title: The verb in second place
goal: Master the most important word-order rule in Danish: the verb always sits in second place, and whatever comes before it pushes the subject behind.
bekal: build statements, questions and sentences that start with an adverbial
hear why *I morgen jeg går* sounds wrong to Danish ears
wave: Go back over **Unit 8** first: read out ten different times, including ones with *halv* and *kvart i*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Weekendplaner
dialogs.intro: Friday afternoon. Ahmad, Mette and Budi make weekend plans while walking home.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: I morgen tager jeg til Malmø. Vil I med?
lines.id: Tomorrow I'm going to Malmö. Do you want to come?
lines.literal: in morning take I to Malmö. will you(pl) with?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Til Sverige? Hvor længe tager toget?
lines.id: To Sweden? How long does the train take?
lines.literal: to Sweden? how long takes train-the?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Kun femogtredive minutter. Så er man der.
lines.id: Only thirty-five minutes. And you're there.
lines.literal: only five-and-thirty minutes. then is one there.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Desværre kan jeg ikke. Jeg arbejder på lørdag.
lines.id: Unfortunately I can't. I'm working on Saturday.
lines.literal: unfortunately can I not. I work on Saturday.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Hvad med søndag? Om søndagen har du fri, ikke?
lines.id: What about Sunday? You're off on Sundays, aren't you?
lines.literal: what with Sunday? on Sunday-the have you free, not?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jo, om søndagen har jeg fri.
lines.literal: yes-indeed, on Sunday-the have I free.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Så tager vi på søndag i stedet.
lines.id: Then we'll go on Sunday instead.
lines.literal: then take we on Sunday in place-the.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Perfekt. Klokken ni mødes vi på hovedbanegården.
lines.id: Perfect. We'll meet at the central station at nine.
lines.literal: perfect. clock-the nine meet we on main-rail-yard-the.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ni? Det er tidligt for en søndag.
lines.id: Nine? That's early for a Sunday.
lines.literal: nine? it is early for a Sunday.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Derfor er det en god idé. Så har vi hele dagen.
lines.id: That's exactly why it's a good idea. Then we have the whole day.
lines.literal: therefore is it a good idea. then have we whole day-the.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Hun har ret. Vi ses på søndag klokken ni!
lines.id: She's right. See you on Sunday at nine!
lines.literal: she has right. we see-each-other on Sunday clock-the nine!

notes: **Count the verbs.** In almost every sentence of this dialogue, the main verb stands in **second place** — not after the subject, but after whatever fills the first slot. Read the dialogue again now and count; that's what this unit trains.

**I morgen tager jeg…** — notice the subject (*jeg*) stands **behind** the verb. English says "Tomorrow I go"; Danish says "Tomorrow go I". If you write *I morgen jeg tager*, you won't be misunderstood, but it instantly sounds foreign.
**Vil I med?** — *med* at the end means "along". A short expression used constantly: *Skal du med?* (Are you coming along?), *Jeg vil gerne med.*

**Jo, not ja.** When the question contains a negation (*har du ikke fri?*, *…ikke?*) and your answer contradicts it with a positive, Danish uses **jo**, not *ja*. English has no such word (you'd say "Yes, I am" or "Oh yes"); German has *doch* and French *si*.
**…, ikke?** at the end of a sentence = "right?", "isn't it?". There's also *…, vel?* and *…, ikke også?*. Very common for asking for agreement — much simpler than English tag questions.
**At have fri** = to be off, to have free time, literally "to have free". Note *fri* stands bare, with no article.

**Hovedbanegården** = the central station, built from *hoved* (head, main) + *bane* (track) + *gård* (yard) + the definite ending *-en*. In Copenhagen people call it *Hovedbanen* or just *Hovedbanegården*.
**Hun har ret** = "she's right". Danish uses *have* here, not *være* — *hun er ret* means nothing.

grammars.title: The second-place rule
body: This single rule decides more than anything else whether your Danish sounds natural — and English only has faint traces of it ("Never have I seen…", "Here comes the bus").

It goes like this: **in a statement, the conjugated verb always takes second place.** The first slot can hold anything — the subject, a time expression, a place, even a whole clause — but as soon as the first slot holds something other than the subject, the subject is pushed to third place.
after: Notice the second column never moves. Whatever happens in the first column, the verb stays in the same place.

⚠️ The most common mistake English speakers make: putting an adverbial first **and still** putting the subject right after it, as in English — *I morgen jeg tager til Malmø.* Danish ears catch it immediately.

How to practice: take an ordinary sentence you already know, move the time expression to the front, and **force yourself to swap** the subject and verb. Repeat ten times with different sentences. After a few days, your ear will do the correcting, not your head.

grammars.title: Questions: the verb moves to the front
body: Because of the second-place rule, Danish questions need no helper word at all — you just move the verb.
after: Compare English, which has to add *do*: *Do you speak Danish?* Danish has no such tool, and that actually makes things simpler.
The question word takes first place, so the verb stays in second place — the rule is consistent, not an exception.

grammars.title: Where ikke goes
body: *Ikke* has a fixed place, and that place is **after** the conjugated verb in a main clause.

head: Sentence
Position of ikke
rows: after the modal, before the main verb
after the subject that has moved
after the subject in a question

after: Other adverbs behave just like *ikke*: *altid*, *aldrig*, *også*, *måske*, *tit*, *heller ikke*. They all stand after the verb: *Jeg cykler **altid** til skole.*

⚠️ There's one place where *ikke* moves **in front of** the verb: inside a subordinate clause. *Jeg ved, at han **ikke kommer**.* The rule gets full treatment in Unit 20; for now just know the exception exists.

sections.title: Linking words that don't change the order

blocks.text: The five linking words below stand **outside the count** — they don't take the first slot, so the clause after them keeps the normal subject-verb order.

head: Linking word
Example
Meaning
rows: Jeg spiser, og jeg drikker kaffe.
Jeg vil gerne, men jeg kan ikke.
Vi tager toget, eller vi cykler.
Jeg bliver hjemme, for jeg er træt.
Det regner, så vi tager bussen.

blocks.text: Compare **derfor** (therefore), which **does** count and so triggers the swap: *Det regner, **derfor tager vi** bussen.* Two words with similar meanings but opposite grammatical effects — watch them closely.

blocks.title: The three-second test
items: Every time you write a Danish sentence, count: what stands in first place? If it isn't the subject, the subject **must** come after the verb.
If your sentence starts with *og*, *men*, *eller*, *for* or *så* — that word doesn't count. Start counting from the word after it.
Three seconds of checking, repeated a few hundred times, is the fastest way to move this rule from your head to your ear.

blocks.text: Danish has **three** words for answering yes/no questions, while English has two. The choice depends on whether the question contains a negation.

The rule is simple: if the question contains *ikke* and your answer contradicts it, use **jo**. Using *ja* there won't be misunderstood, but it's one of the quickest signs that someone hasn't been learning for long.

Notice also that short Danish answers use *det gør jeg* ("that do I") — much like English *I do*. The form follows the verb: *Er du træt? — Ja, **det er jeg**.* / *Har du tid? — Nej, **det har jeg ikke**.*

exercises.prompt: Rewrite each sentence with the time expression first.
items: Jeg tager til Malmø i morgen.
Hun arbejder på en café om lørdagen.
Vi mødes på stationen klokken ni.
Han cykler til skole hver dag.

exercises.prompt: Put ikke in the right place. Write each sentence out in full.
Fill in ja, jo or nej.
items: Kommer du ikke i morgen? — ____, jeg kommer.
Bor hun i København? — ____, hun bor i Aarhus.

answers: I morgen tager jeg til Malmø. — Om lørdagen arbejder hun på en café. — Klokken ni mødes vi på stationen. — Hver dag cykler han til skole. — Om aftenen spiser de sammen.
Taler du dansk? — Bor hun i Aarhus? — Kommer de i morgen? — Har han fri på søndag? — Arbejder I her?
Jeg taler ikke dansk. — Han kommer ikke i dag. — Jeg kan ikke tale dansk. — I morgen kommer jeg ikke. — Kommer du ikke?
